subject: english-language
topicDisplay: Unit 1 Writing For Purpose And Audience And Reading To Access Non Fiction And Media Texts
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the assessment objectives.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which sentence uses the most ambitious, precise vocabulary?
options: The house was very very scary.
The derelict mansion loomed, its decaying facade menacing the street.
The old house was scary and big.
The big house was really old and bad.
questions.explain: 'Derelict', 'loomed', 'decaying' and 'menacing' are precise, ambitious word choices.

questions.q: To SYNTHESISE information from two sources, you should:
options: List every word in both texts
Combine relevant points from both into a single, linked explanation
questions.explain: Synthesis means drawing together and connecting information from both texts.

questions.q: Which is an effective way to vary sentence length for tension in narrative writing?
options: Follow several longer sentences with a short, punchy one: 'He stopped.'
questions.explain: A sudden short sentence after longer ones creates emphasis and tension.

questions.q: A travel article says "You will love every breathtaking moment of this paradise." What is its main PURPOSE?
options: To persuade the reader to visit
questions.explain: Positive, emotive language directed at "you" is designed to persuade the reader to go.

questions.q: Which of these is a FACT rather than an opinion?
options: The film is too long and dull
This is the best film ever made
questions.explain: A runtime can be checked and verified, making it a fact; the others are judgements.

questions.q: A writer shares a short personal story about losing their dog to illustrate a point. This technique is an:
questions.explain: A brief personal story used to support an argument is an anecdote.

questions.q: "Over 90% of teachers agree that homework helps." Which persuasive device is used here?
questions.explain: A figure or percentage used to support a point is a statistic.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of a discourse marker such as 'however' or 'furthermore'?
options: To signal the relationship between ideas and guide the reader
questions.explain: Discourse markers connect ideas and show contrast, addition or sequence to aid coherence.

questions.q: Which is the clearest sign of the intended AUDIENCE in "Top tips for surviving your first term at uni"?
options: It is aimed at retired people
Casual language and the reference to "uni" suggest young/new students
questions.explain: Informal tone and student-focused content signal a young, new-undergraduate audience.

questions.q: For an article aimed at teenagers about social media, which register is most suitable?
options: A lively, accessible tone with some direct address
questions.explain: Matching register to a teenage audience means engaging but clear, not stuffy or patronising.

questions.q: A writer's TONE in "Honestly, what a complete and utter shambles this has become" is best described as:
questions.explain: The dismissive phrasing conveys scorn and frustration.

questions.q: In the persuasive acronym DAFOREST, what does the 'F' stand for?
questions.explain: DAFOREST stands for Direct address, Alliteration, Facts, Opinions, Rhetorical questions, Emotive language, Statistics, Triplets.
